lessons.title: The butterfly and angles
lessons.objective: Explain the goalie's stance and how they cut down angles.

payload.prompt: Identify the butterfly save position.

image.alt: Goalie in butterfly position, pads flared to seal the ice.

options.text: Butterfly: knees down, pads flared outward.
Upright stance with pads together.
One leg extended to block the perimeter.

explanation.correct: Right. Butterfly is knees down, pads flared, sealing the net.
explanation.incorrect: The butterfly position drops both knees and spreads the pads wide.
explanation.sayThisLine: Butterfly covers the bottom of the net.

payload.prompt: Tap the goalie's best position to cut angles.

diagram.alt: Top-down view of goalie positioning to cut shooter angles.

explanation.correct: Right. Optimal depth cuts the angle without overcommitting.
explanation.incorrect: The goalie cuts angles by challenging out, but not so far that he is vulnerable.
explanation.sayThisLine: Position between the puck and the goal.

payload.prompt: A shooter at the circle stays unchallenged. The goalie sits deep. Smart?

scene.alt: Goalie positioning deep in the crease while a shooter approaches.

explanation.correct: False. Challenging cuts the angle and forces a rushed shot.
explanation.incorrect: Staying deep gives the shooter more time and space to find an opening.

payload.prompt: Why does the butterfly position create rebounds?

options.text: Hard pads bounce pucks instead of absorbing them.
The goalie's chest is exposed in this position.
Goalies cannot move quickly out of the butterfly.
Shots pass through the goalie in the butterfly.

explanation.correct: Right. Pads bounce pucks; gloves absorb. Rebounds are the trade-off.
explanation.incorrect: The butterfly pads are hard and smooth, so they bounce shots forward.
explanation.sayThisLine: Butterfly pads bounce pucks. Control the rebound.

statement.speaker: Color commentator
statement.text: That goalie plays too deep. He is giving up angles.

payload.question: What angle problem does the commentator see?

options.text: Staying deep gives the shooter a bigger view.
options.explanation: Correct. Deep play = more net to aim at.

options.text: The goalie's pads are positioned wrong.
options.explanation: It is about positioning depth, not pad angle.

options.text: The goalie lets the shooter close in too much.
options.explanation: The opposite: challenge out to reduce the angle.

payload.translation: Playing too deep in the crease gives shooters more of the net.

followUps.line: Good positioning shrinks the target. Challenge out.
followUps.why: Understands the goal of angle management.

followUps.line: Depth balance: too far out and you lose to a deke.
Great goalies make positioning look natural.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Angles are subtle. Video review teaches you this.

lessons.title: Rebounds and second chances
lessons.objective: Explain rebound control and why second chances score.

payload.prompt: A save creates a big rebound. Is the second shot more dangerous?

scene.alt: Goalie deflecting a shot; puck bounces loose in front.

explanation.correct: True. Rebound = forward set up, close to net, loose puck.
explanation.incorrect: A rebound is a gift. The forward is right on it.

payload.prompt: How does a goalie prevent big rebounds?

options.text: Absorb the shot with glove or chest.
Punch the puck high into the air.
Keep the pads flat to let pucks slide off.
Kick the puck to the corner immediately.

explanation.correct: Right. Absorb to deaden it. Bounce to lose it.
explanation.incorrect: Soft parts (glove, chest) kill rebounds. Hard pads bounce them.

payload.prompt: Slot rebounds are the riskiest because the net is close.
payload.template: A rebound in the {{area}} goes in before {{who}} {{when}}.

explanation.correct: Perfect. Slot rebounds are tap-in city.
explanation.incorrect: The slot is where goals happen. A rebound there is a second chance on ice.

payload.prompt: Order how a slot rebound becomes a goal.

items.text: Shot bounces off goalie into the slot.
items.why: Initial shot creates the rebound in scoring area.

items.text: Forward moves to puck while goalie recovers.
items.why: Forward has a split second while goalie is sliding.

items.text: Quick tap-in or snap shot beats the goalie.

explanation.incorrect: A careless rebound gives the forward a tap-in. Control it.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: He made the save but leaked a juicy rebound to the slot.

payload.question: What did the goalie do wrong?

options.text: Did not control the rebound properly.
options.explanation: Correct. A loose puck in scoring position is a mistake.

options.text: Did not make the first save.
options.explanation: He made the save. The problem is the rebound.

options.text: Should have called a timeout.
options.explanation: Rebound control is a skill, not a timeout situation.

payload.translation: A good save is wasted if the rebound lands in scoring range.

followUps.line: Goalie work continues after the initial save.
followUps.why: Work is not done on the save.

followUps.line: Forwards hunt rebounds. Do not feed them.
Save % does not measure rebound control.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Rebound control is an art. Watch goalies who own it.

lessons.title: Save percentage, GAA and limits
lessons.objective: Read goalie stats and understand what they measure.

payload.prompt: Rate a .915 save percentage in the modern NHL.

explanation.correct: Good save percentage. .910 is average; .915 is solid.
explanation.incorrect: In the modern NHL, .910 is average. .915 is above it.

payload.prompt: Save percentage alone does not tell you shot quality?

options.text: It misses the quality of shots faced.
It ignores team winning record.
It does not account for goalie height.
It misses games played.

explanation.correct: Right. .910 against good defense is different from .910 against bad defense.
explanation.incorrect: Save percentage counts saves divided by shots, but ignores shot quality.

payload.prompt: Goals Against Average per 60 minutes.
payload.template: GAA is {{what}}, but it is {{useful}} because {{reason}}.

explanation.correct: Exactly. GAA depends on the defense in front.
explanation.incorrect: GAA (goals per 60 min) is affected by defense. Save % is cleaner.

payload.prompt: Match the goalie stat to what it measures.

pairs.definition: Team result, not just the goalie.

explanation.summary: Save % is cleanest. GAA and wins need context.
explanation.sayThisLine: Save percentage is about the goalie alone.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: Our goalie has lower GAA, so ours is better.

payload.question: Why might this conclusion be wrong?

options.text: The other team's defense might be worse.
options.explanation: Correct. GAA depends on defense. Look at context.

options.text: GAA is not counted in modern hockey.
options.explanation: GAA is still tracked, just not reliable alone.

options.text: Never compare goalies by stats.
options.explanation: Stats help. Just look at the right ones.

payload.translation: Lower GAA might mean better defense, not better goalie.

followUps.line: Save % is more portable between teams.
followUps.why: Understands what makes a good metric.

followUps.line: Strong defense makes every goalie look good.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Goalie comparison is hard. Context always matters.

lessons.title: Goals saved above expected
lessons.objective: Explain how shot quality reveals true skill.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: His save percentage is .910 but xG is terrible. Stealing games.

payload.question: What does this comparison show?

options.text: Stopping hard chances better than the model predicts.
options.explanation: Correct. High save % on tough chances = outperforming.

options.text: Defense is excellent.
options.explanation: The analysis is about the goalie, not defense.

options.text: He got lucky and will regress.
options.explanation: Maybe, but outperformance can signal skill.

payload.translation: When save % is high on difficult shots, the goalie is exceeding expectations.

followUps.line: GSAx (goals saved above expected) measures outperformance.
Positive GSAx suggests skill in positioning.
followUps.why: Shows understanding of what it means.

followUps.line: Over time, GSAx is more stable than luck.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Advanced stats are evolving. Your intuition still counts.

payload.prompt: xG against is 2.5, goals allowed are 1.5. Is he outperforming?

scene.alt: Comparison of expected vs actual goals scored.

explanation.correct: True. Model says 2.5, only 1.5 scored. Outperforming.
explanation.incorrect: If model expects 2.5 and 1.5 went in, the goalie is beating the model.

payload.prompt: Goalie A: .900 SV%, Goalie B: .905 SV%. But A faced harder chances. Who is better?

situation.narrative: Both have similar save percentages, different shot quality.

facts.label: Context
facts.value: A: hard chances; B: easy chances

options.label: Goalie A (harder chances)
options.consequence: Harder work deserves credit. But .900 is below average.

options.label: Goalie B (higher SV%)
options.consequence: Higher save % on any load is a clear win.

options.label: Impossible to tell
options.consequence: Avoid saying impossible. Numbers tell you something.

payload.expertNote: Context helps, but higher save % on any shot load is a plus.
payload.sayThisLine: Higher save percentage on any load is good.

payload.prompt: Goals saved above expected (GSAx) compares performance.
payload.template: GSAx compares {{who}} to {{what}}, and positive means {{outcome}}.

explanation.correct: Perfect. GSAx measures beating the model.
explanation.incorrect: GSAx compares actual performance to shot-quality prediction.

lessons.title: Starters, backups and rest
lessons.objective: Explain goalie rotation and why rest matters.

payload.prompt: Back-to-back nights, home then away. Starter is hot. Play him twice?

situation.narrative: Back-to-back set; starter in great form.

facts.label: Backup
facts.value: Fresh but no games in two weeks

options.label: Play starter both nights
options.consequence: Maximize win odds, but overwork risks fatigue.
considerations: One loss to save the goalie is smart

options.label: Rest starter second night
options.consequence: Smart management. Backup gets work. Save the star.
considerations: One loss now, healthy goalie later

options.label: Starter tonight, backup tomorrow
options.consequence: Compromise. You get one win, but backup is cold.
considerations: Backup is rusty in game two

payload.expertNote: Rest your star on back-to-backs. One game beats a worn-down goalie.
payload.sayThisLine: Rest the starter. One game is worth health.

payload.prompt: A backup's job is rest and readiness.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Backup gets rests and stays sharp.
explanation.incorrect: A backup plays 10-15 games: back-to-backs, rest days, injuries.

payload.prompt: Match the workload role to its meaning.

pairs.definition: Plays 10-15 games; rests and fills in.

explanation.summary: Smart teams use their backups to rest the starter.

payload.prompt: Five games in seven days. What is the biggest risk?

options.text: Goalie will demand a trade.
Fatigue hurts focus and positioning.
Backup will challenge for the job.
Automatic contract bonus.

explanation.correct: Right. Tired goalie = worse angles and reads.
explanation.incorrect: Overwork hurts the little things that make you good.

statement.speaker: Coach
statement.text: Three back-to-backs this month. I need smart workload management.

payload.question: What is the coach planning?

options.text: Resting starter on some back-to-back nights.
Firing the backup if he does not perform.
Making the team play fewer games.
options.explanation: The schedule is fixed. The coach is managing what exists.

payload.translation: Workload management = using the backup on back-to-backs.

followUps.line: A tired goalie in March hurts more than one game.
Good backup depth is crucial for this.
Coaches balance: rest star, keep backup sharp.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Coaches trade short wins for long health.

lessons.title: Interference and challenges
lessons.objective: Understand the rule and when to challenge.

payload.prompt: Attacker in crease, no hard contact, puck at his feet. Interference?

scene.alt: Attacker standing in crease with loose puck nearby.

explanation.correct: True. Being in the crease and blocking the goalie's movement.
explanation.incorrect: Crease contact that prevents a save is interference.

payload.prompt: Goal called. You think interference. Challenge or accept?

situation.narrative: Goal was just called. Replays look close.

facts.label: Replay
facts.value: Light contact, unclear if it prevented save

options.label: Challenge for interference
options.consequence: 50-50 call. If you win, keep timeout. If you lose, it is gone.

options.label: Accept the goal
options.consequence: Save timeout for a clearer situation later.
considerations: One goal is not worth it

options.label: Yell at the referee
options.consequence: No change to call. Might get a penalty.

payload.expertNote: Interference is judgment-heavy. Challenges rarely work on borderline calls.
payload.sayThisLine: Save the timeout for an obvious one.

payload.prompt: What is the key question in an interference review?

options.text: Did the attacker touch the goalie?
Did it prevent a save the goalie would have made?
Was the attacker in the crease?
Did the attacker have clear view of net?

explanation.correct: Right. Did it prevent a save? That is the question.
explanation.incorrect: Interference is whether it prevented a save, not just contact.

statement.speaker: Broadcaster
statement.text: Minimal contact but the goalie could not get across. That is interference.

payload.question: What is the broadcaster suggesting?

options.text: Light contact can still prevent a save.
options.explanation: Correct. Interference is about impact on the save, not force.

options.text: Any contact is automatic interference.
options.explanation: Not automatic. Must prevent a save.

options.text: Broadcaster thinks goal should stand.

payload.translation: Interference depends on whether contact prevented the goalie.

followUps.line: Video review looks for objective facts, not fairness.
Interference is the most reviewed call.
Legally screen and do not contact the goalie.
followUps.why: The legal way to help your team.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Interference is controversial. Borderline cases are tough.

payload.prompt: Order how a review happens after a goal.

items.text: Goal is called on the ice.
Refs confirm goal or wave it off.

explanation.correct: Perfect. Goal, challenge, review, decision, penalty.
explanation.incorrect: Coach must challenge quickly. Failed challenge = lost timeout.
